title: Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models
pub: Journal of Legal Analysis, vol. 16, no. 1, pp. 64-93 (2024)
author: Matthew Dahl · Varun Magesh · Mirac Suzgun · Daniel E. Ho

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source does not directly assess whether human oversight provides effective control, independent verification, or adequate professional guidance. Instead, it reframes the principal concern around empirical evaluation of LLM legal knowledge and hallucination, arguing that access-to-justice benefits depend on models actually knowing the law and distributing that knowledge evenly.
qs: As one highly influential but still maturing species of AI, LLMs stand in need of a concrete empirical evaluation of their legal abilities and their legal risks, of which hallucination is certainly one.
This potential can only be realized, however, if LLMs actually know the law.

It provides no findings, reasoning or recommendations showing whether the source accepts or rejects the cluster’s proposition that cheaper AI assistance may increase participation without improving remedies.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied source material contains only bibliography entries and no substantive claims, methods, findings, or recommendations. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine whether the source accepts, extends, redirects, or opposes the cluster’s proposition about evaluating realistic professional task execution and validating scoring methods.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source accepts that legal hallucinations require scrutiny and extends the cluster’s emphasis on task-dependent reliability by proposing systematic study across doctrine, courts, jurisdictions and time, as well as directional errors and latent biases. It contributes a research agenda rather than empirical findings or measured error rates.
qs: Are LLMs equally familiar with different dimensions of the American common law system—where legal doctrine varies across courts, jurisdictions, and over time—or do they tend to hallucinate more in certain areas than others?

And besides hallucination itself, are there other features of LLMs that legal scholars need to consider—other latent biases or behavioral tendencies that threaten to spill over into downstream applications of these models?

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source strongly accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially strengthens it with a large, structured evaluation showing frequent, task-dependent factual errors in public LLMs. It also develops the proposition by showing systematic overconfidence, uneven legal knowledge and vulnerability to false premises, while concluding that mitigation remains promising but does not justify unsupervised reliance and that users should verify outputs.
qs: Performance degrades fur- ther on the most complex Core legal question and Central holding tasks, with hallucinations arising in response to at least 59% and 63% of our queries, respectively.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-centred, selective-deployment proposition and materially strengthens it with large-scale evidence that open-domain legal knowledge is unreliable, errors vary by task complexity and court level, and model confidence is imperfectly calibrated. It therefore supports experienced, verified augmentation rather than unsupervised legal use.
qs: Performing the first systematic empirical test of popular perceptions (Roberts 2023; Romoser 2023; Weiser 2023), we show that factual legal hallucinations are widespread in the LLMs that we study—OpenAI’s ChatGPT 4, OpenAI’s ChatGPT 3.5, Google’s PaLM 2, and Meta’s Llama 2—on the bulk of the legal knowledge tasks that we profile (Section 5.1).

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The study supports the cluster’s distinction between bounded model capability and dependable autonomous legal work. Its systematic findings of frequent hallucinations, poor confidence calibration and acceptance of false premises directly reinforce the cluster’s citation-reliability concerns and its case for supervised, task-specific deployment rather than inference from headline benchmark performance.
qs: Using OpenAI’s ChatGPT 4 and other public models, we show that LLMs hallucinate at least 58% of the time, struggle to pre- dict their own hallucinations, and often uncritically accept users’ incorrect legal assumptions.
We conclude by cautioning against the rapid and unsupervised integration of popular LLMs into legal tasks, and we develop a typology of legal hallucinations to guide future research in this area.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that promising performance on discrete legal tasks does not establish dependable legal competence and that hallucinations can make legal assistance harmful. Although it claims a systematic empirical contribution, the supplied material provides no results or reform recommendations, so it does not materially extend the cluster’s conclusions about verification, access to justice or regulatory boundaries.

kp.k: Public-facing models frequently hallucinated federal case-law information
kp.d: Dahl, Magesh, Suzgun and Ho report pooled reference-based hallucination rates of 58% for GPT 4, 69% for GPT 3.5, 72% for PaLM 2 and 88% for Llama 2. These are findings about the tested off-the-shelf models and legal knowledge queries, not measured error rates for specialist legal research products or future models. The study tested gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-3.5-turbo-0613, text-bison-001 and Llama-2-13b-chat-hf.
qs: when asked a direct, verifiable question about a randomly selected federal court case, LLMs hallucinate between 58% (ChatGPT 4) and 88% (Llama 2) of the time.
We perform our experiments using four popular, state-of-the-art, off-the-shelf LLMs:

kp.k: Large-scale testing distinguished factual errors from other hallucinations
kp.d: The researchers developed fourteen tasks and sampled 5,000 published cases from each federal judicial level, stratifying Supreme Court cases by year, appellate cases by circuit-year and district cases by state-year. Main samples covered SCOTUS 1794–2015, USCOA 1895–2019 and USDC 1932–2019. They executed more than 800,000 queries. Their empirical focus was factual fidelity to law, distinguishing this from fidelity to prompts or training material; the resulting assessment addresses embedded legal knowledge rather than establishing performance across every legal reasoning or professional task.
qs: We draw 5,000 cases from each level of the judiciary.
we execute more than 800,000 queries—200,000+ per LLM
the third way that an LLM can hallucinate is by producing a response that lacks fidelity to the facts of the world

kp.k: Abstention and prompting materially affect interpretation of error rates
kp.d: Reference-based tasks compared primarily temperature-zero responses with external metadata, counting explicit abstention as non-hallucination rather than correctness. Although the main discussion emphasizes few-shot results, the appendix reports lower pooled zero-shot rates, largely because models abstained more. This is particularly important for quotations: GPT 4 and GPT 3.5 abstained on 99.9% and 100% respectively of zero-shot appellate and district quotation queries. Low hallucination therefore need not indicate successful completion of legal work.
qs: we nevertheless count the response as a non-hallucination
These changes are largely driven by abstentions in the Quotation and the more complex tasks
One exception is the zero-shot Quotation task, where many LLMs abstain.

kp.k: Complex legal synthesis exposed substantial knowledge limitations
kp.d: The authors find increasing difficulty as tasks move from case metadata to substantive opinion content and synthesis. Few-shot doctrinal-agreement error rates in Table 5 were 0.449 for GPT 4, 0.458 for GPT 3.5, 0.453 for PaLM 2 and 0.500 for Llama 2, indicating limited improvement over guessing on this binary task. Five more complex tasks used 100 cases per judicial level and contradictions between two temperature-one responses, assessed by GPT 4. The authors characterize these estimates as lower bounds because repeated, mutually consistent falsehoods are not detected; human validation on 100 queries produced Cohen’s κ of 0.87 and 0.77 against GPT 4, compared with 0.79 between human coders.
qs: Hallucinations then surge among the moderate complexity tasks
represent little improvement over random guessing, and are actually sometimes worse.
two answers may be logically consonant but still lack fidelity to the law.

kp.k: Knowledge varies across courts, jurisdictions, prominence and time
kp.d: Aggregated results were strongest for Supreme Court cases and weakest for district court cases. Among post-1981 appellate decisions, performance was strongest in the Ninth, Second, Third and First Circuits; the D.C. Circuit performed worst despite its perceived influence. Supreme Court hallucinations declined sharply above the 90th prominence percentile for GPT 4, GPT 3.5 and PaLM 2. Temporal performance was nonlinear: the oldest and newest cases were most problematic, with the lowest rates for Warren Court cases from 1953–1969. These are observed associations, which the authors interpret as limitations on localized and current legal knowledge.
qs: our LLMs perform best on tasks at the SCOTUS level, worse on tasks at the USCOA level, and worst on tasks at the USDC level.
a sharp slope change occurs around the 90th prominence percentile
LLMs’ peak performance may lag several years behind the current state of the doctrine

kp.k: False premises often elicited fabricated legal answers
kp.d: The researchers tested nonexistent dissents and alleged overrulings of cases that had never been overruled. Pooled contra-factual hallucination rates were 69% for GPT 4, 52% for GPT 3.5, 99% for PaLM 2 and 2% for Llama 2. Llama 2’s apparent advantage requires qualification: its rejections sometimes falsely denied that real cases or justices existed, but these were counted as successful premise rejections under this task’s metric. The authors identify particular risks for inexperienced researchers and pro se litigants who may not recognize errors in their own questions.
qs: any uncritical answering of the prompt is treated as a hallucination.
Llama 2 often states that the case or justice does not exist at all.
we choose to record these examples as successful rejections of the premise.

kp.k: Confidence did not reliably distinguish accurate legal answers
kp.d: Confidence was estimated from agreement between ten temperature-one samples and a greedy response, rather than simply from models’ verbal confidence claims. Pooled expected calibration errors were 0.057 for PaLM 2, 0.099 for GPT 3.5, 0.190 for GPT 4 and 0.421 for Llama 2. Thus, the least hallucination-prone model was not the best calibrated. Ex post scaling reduced pooled errors to 0.049, 0.051, 0.033 and 0.035 respectively, but the authors report residual problems; Llama 2’s improvement largely reflected compressing confidence into the 0.0–0.3 interval.
qs: although GPT 4 is our best performing model in terms of raw hallucination rates (Figure 1), it is actually less calibrated than PaLM 2 and GPT 3.5
Not only may they receive a hallucinated response, but they may receive one that the LLM is overconfident in and liable to repeat again.
the rescaled Llama 2 model is simply not confident in any of its responses.

kp.k: Access-to-justice benefits remain conditional on reliable legal knowledge
kp.d: The authors acknowledge the promise of cheap, quick legal assistance but argue that observed weaknesses disproportionately threaten under-resourced and pro se litigants, especially those needing localized or complex information, asking mistaken questions or struggling to judge trustworthiness. They warn that widespread use could exacerbate existing inequalities and propagate a legal monoculture favoring prominent cases, jurisdictions and judges. These are implications and prospective risks drawn from the model results, not direct measurements of litigant outcomes or legal-market inequality.
qs: we find that the risks are highest for those who would benefit from LLMs most
Some of these risks—namely, (3) and (4)—might be mitigated with improved user education, but others—(1) and (2)—are more intractable.
producing a falsely homogenous sense of the legal landscape.

kp.k: Technical mitigation offers promise but does not guarantee reliability
kp.d: Reporting other research rather than conducting their own mitigation comparison, the authors discuss retrieval-augmented generation, advanced prompting, fine-tuning, decoding methods and external database checks. They caution that retrieval depends on source quality, database updating and distinguishing binding law from outdated or jurisdictionally irrelevant authorities. They also argue that fidelity to prompts, training corpora and legal facts can conflict, requiring transparent developer choices rather than solely technical optimization.
qs: the effectiveness of RAG-based methods heavily relies on the quality of their retrieval mechanisms
it is far from clear whether these technical improvements will be able to truly solve the hallucination problem.
developers of legal LLMs will need to make choices about which type(s) of hallucinations to minimize

kp.k: Responsible deployment should augment humans and retain verification
kp.d: The authors recommend vigilance by experienced practitioners, including checking prompts and model responses, and caution legal scholars and educators against importing subtle knowledge biases into research and teaching. They advocate augmentation rather than unsupervised reliance on model-generated law. They also release queries and answers for future benchmarking, recognizing that subsequent model capabilities require continuing assessment.
qs: more experienced legal practitioners may find some value in consulting LLMs for certain tasks
our findings underscore the importance of human-centered AI.
Responsible integration of LLMs into legal tasks must augment lawyers, researchers, and litigants
we release a test dataset of our queries and answers on the HuggingFace platform

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dahl, Magesh, Suzgun and Ho argue that factual unreliability limits off-the-shelf LLMs as sources of legal advice, supports supervised augmentation rather than unsupervised reliance, and could worsen inequalities in legal services.
pts.d: The authors report widespread errors in the tested models' knowledge of federal case law, weaker performance on substantive legal tasks, susceptibility to false premises, and imperfect calibration. They argue that improvements in legal reasoning alone cannot compensate for missing legal knowledge. They predict that uneven knowledge across jurisdictions, periods and judges could produce a legal monoculture and propagate biases through downstream applications. These service-level consequences are interpretations and prospective risks, not measured changes in client outcomes. They acknowledge potential value in selected tasks but advocate human-centered use with checking of prompts and responses.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest primarily on a large empirical evaluation of four general-purpose models, with downstream service implications inferred from the observed failures.
pts.d: The authors develop fourteen tasks, draw stratified samples of 5,000 cases from each federal judicial level, and execute more than 800,000 queries. Reference-based tasks use external case metadata; the headline pooled hallucination rates are 58% for GPT 4, 69% for GPT 3.5, 72% for PaLM 2 and 88% for Llama 2. Abstentions count as non-hallucinations, not correct answers. Five higher-complexity tasks use repeated-response contradiction detection, which the authors describe as yielding lower bounds; GPT 4's contradiction labels are checked against two human coders on 100 queries. False-dissent and false-overruling experiments test acceptance of erroneous premises. Calibration is estimated from repeated sampling rather than users' judgments or merely the models' verbal confidence: pooled expected calibration errors are 0.190, 0.099, 0.057 and 0.421 respectively. These are findings about the named off-the-shelf models, not commercial legal research products, Harvey, or legal-AI systems generally. Predictions about access inequalities and downstream bias also draw on cited scholarship; the study does not directly measure professional productivity, legal-service prices, employment or litigant outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The conclusions concern the model versions evaluated for the 2024 paper; future improvements are acknowledged without a deadline for reliable autonomous legal advice.
pts.d: The tested versions are gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-3.5-turbo-0613, text-bison-001 and Llama-2-13b-chat-hf. The principal case samples cover SCOTUS decisions from 1794–2015, appellate decisions from 1895–2019 and district decisions from 1932–2019, with different periods for specialized tasks. The study tests open-domain legal knowledge, rather than document-grounded summarization or retrieval-augmented legal products. Reference-based responses generally use temperature zero; contradiction-based tasks use temperature one. Main discussion emphasizes few-shot results; the appendix reports lower zero-shot aggregate rates driven partly by abstention. The authors acknowledge promising mitigation through retrieval, prompting, fine-tuning, decoding and external checks, but condition success on retrieval quality, current databases, treatment of conflicting authorities, and reliable evaluation. They identify normative tensions among fidelity to prompts, training data and legal facts. Post-hoc calibration improves results but does not remove all stated challenges. No date is predicted for resolving these limitations.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify under-resourced and self-represented litigants as especially exposed, while practitioners, researchers, educators and developers also face distinct responsibilities and risks.
pts.d: Litigants seeking localized or complex information, posing mistaken questions, or lacking the expertise to judge responses are particularly vulnerable. The authors infer that this could undermine the access-to-justice benefits of inexpensive legal information. Experienced lawyers may still obtain task-specific value but must check both prompts and outputs; no verification time or cost is quantified. Scholars and educators risk incorporating knowledge biases into research and teaching. Developers must make choices about competing forms of fidelity and disclose them to downstream users. The authors also suggest that resource-rich actors have an advantage in building private legal models, while arguing that resources alone do not settle the conceptual trade-offs. They do not predict staffing reductions, changes to firm leverage, billing-model replacement or market shares.
